finding.claim: Missing authorization on file deletion. The delete route imports the boolean predicate is_allowed under the alias require_allowed and ignores its return value. Every caller, including users with no grants, can delete any file.
finding.source: Any HTTP client sending DELETE /files/<fid>, with any or no X-Session-User-Verified header, and a known or guessed fid.

trace.note: from acl import is_allowed as require_allowed. This is the non-enforcing bool predicate, not ensure_allowed.
f = STORE[fid] looks up the resource.
require_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') returns False for unauthorized users, but the result is discarded and abort(403) is never called.
is_allowed only returns a bool. Only ensure_allowed (acl.py:8) aborts.

finding.guards_checked: The rename route correctly uses ensure_allowed (views.py:26), but the delete route does not. There is no other decorator, middleware or check on the delete path. The before_request hook only sets g.user and does not enforce anything.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: is_allowed (acl.py:4) returns a bool only and its result is discarded at views.py:18. The before_request hook (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8) aborts but is not called in the delete route.
verdict.reason: views.py:4 aliases the bool predicate is_allowed as require_allowed, views.py:18 calls it as a bare statement with the result discarded, and views.py:19 then runs del STORE[fid] for any caller, including anonymous ones.

verdict_facts.guard_found: none (is_allowed bool predicate imported as require_allowed; its result is discarded; before_request only sets g.user)
verdict_facts.reason: views.py:4 aliases the bool-returning is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) as require_allowed, views.py:18 calls it as a bare statement without abort, so views.py:19 `del STORE[fid]` runs for any caller, unlike rename which uses the aborting ensure_allowed (views.py:26, acl.py:8-10).

finding.claim: Authentication is taken from a client-controlled request header. g.user comes straight from X-Session-User-Verified with no signature or session validation in this code. Unless a trusted front proxy strips and sets this header, an attacker can impersonate any user who has grants, and can then pass the ensure_allowed check on rename.
finding.source: The attacker sets the HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified: <victim-user>. This assumes the app is reachable without a header-sanitizing proxy.
finding.sink: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, 'write') followed by f['name'] = request.json['name'] (views.py:26-27). The same applies to any other ACL decision.

trace.note: The ACL check uses g.user as the identity.
The grants lookup is keyed by that unverified string.

finding.guards_checked: No signature, session or token verification exists in the repository. The header name implies an upstream proxy sets it, but nothing in this code enforces that the header is stripped from client input. This finding is conditional on that deployment assumption.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 when grants don't include the user, but it is keyed on the attacker-controlled g.user. No authentication, signature or session check and no header-stripping exists in the repo (only views.py and acl.py).
verdict.reason: views.py:12 sets g.user straight from the client header, and views.py:26 passes it to ensure_allowed, which only does a dict lookup on that string (acl.py:5), so an anonymous attacker who sends a grantee's name passes the check and reaches the rename write at views.py:27 (this assumes no header-sanitizing proxy sits in front of the app). Separately, delete_file at views.py:18 calls the boolean is_allowed under the alias require_allowed and discards the result, so DELETE has no ACL check at all; that is a different bug from this finding.

verdict_facts.guard_found: The `X-Session-User-Verified` header read at views.py:12 is treated as trusted identity from upstream middleware under the stated project facts. `ensure_allowed` (acl.py:8-10) aborts with 403 when `is_allowed` fails, and it is called correctly at views.py:26.
verdict_facts.reason: The trace is accurate (views.py:12 sets g.user from the header, views.py:26 calls ensure_allowed, acl.py:5 looks up grants by that string, views.py:27 writes the name). But the maintainer states that request identity such as g.user is populated by trusted upstream middleware, and the finding depends on that assumption being false, so it is not a vulnerability in this code. Separately, `delete_file` at views.py:18 calls `is_allowed` aliased as `require_allowed` and discards the result, so any request can delete any file. The candidate did not report that bug.

finding.claim: Unhandled KeyError and TypeError conditions. STORE[fid] raises KeyError for an unknown id, and request.json['name'] raises on a missing or malformed body. Both produce 500 errors. This is a low-severity robustness and existence-oracle issue, and it is not a directly exploitable vulnerability.
finding.source: A request to /files/<unknown-fid>, or a rename POST with no 'name' key or a non-JSON body.
finding.sink: Unhandled exceptions, giving 500 versus 403 responses that reveal whether an fid exists. The 500 is returned before the authorization check.

trace.note: STORE[fid] raises KeyError before any authorization check.

finding.guards_checked: No error handlers and no input validation are present.

verdict.guard_found: none (no error handlers or input validation; the before_request hook at views.py:10-12 only reads a header)
verdict.reason: views.py:17 and views.py:25 do `STORE[fid]` with no existence check or error handler, so an unknown fid raises KeyError and returns a 500 before any ACL call, and views.py:27 indexes `request.json["name"]` unvalidated; this is a low-severity robustness issue and existence oracle, reachable by any caller including an anonymous one. Note that in recent Flask versions a non-JSON body gives a 415 or 400 rather than a 500, but a missing "name" key still gives a 500.

verdict_facts.guard_found: none (no error handlers or input validation; the only authorization checks run after the lookup)
verdict_facts.reason: views.py:17 and :25 do `STORE[fid]` before any authorization check, and views.py:27 does `request.json["name"]` without validation. An unknown fid or a malformed body therefore gives an unhandled exception (500), and a 500 for unknown ids versus a 403 or success for known ids reveals whether an fid exists. Severity is low. Separately, views.py:18 uses `require_allowed`, which is an alias for the bool-returning `is_allowed` (acl.py:4), and discards the result. That is a different, stronger bug, and it does not affect this finding.
